la:verb:exaro.gloss: to plough or dig up; till, cultivate, plough
senses: to plough or dig up; till, cultivate, plough
to write, note or set down something on tablets
la:verb:exaro.html:
ex-ăro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to plough or dig up (class.).
Lit.: radices, Cato. R. R. 61; id. ap. ; : sepulcra,: terminos (with deicere),: deum, puerum,; . —
Transf.
To raise, produce by tillage: tantum frumenti, ut, etc.,; cf. Zumpt,.—
In gen., to plough, till, cultivate, ; : locum de integro,: agrum,: viam publicam,; with effodere mala,i. e. to dig up the earth about them,.—Poet.: cum rugis vetus frontem senectus exaret, furrows, wrinkles, * (cf. aro).—
To write, note, set down something on tablets (used by Cic. only in his letters): undecimo die postquam a te discesseram, hoc literularum

exaravi, ; cf. ; : novum prooemium,: ad te harum exemplum in codicillis,; cf.: binos codicillos,: id ipsum his versibus exaravi, etc.,; cf.: librum tertium Aesopi stilo,: versus,; .—

Latera, to flog severely, .

la:verb:exacuo.html:
ex-ăcŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.,
to make very sharp, to sharpen, make pointed (class.).
Lit.: ferramenta cote,; : ridicas,: vallos furcasque bicornes,: spicula,: dentes,: metas in angustissimas vertices,: cornua in leve fastigium, et saep.—
Transf., of taste: aceto exacuendo,for making pungent,; of the sight: aciem oculorum,; cf. visum,.—
Trop.
In gen.: nisi mucronem aliquem tribunitium exacuisset in nos,: (cum animus) exacuerit illam ut oculorum sic ingenii aciem ad bona diligenda,; cf. animum,: morbos, i. e. to aggravate, Col. poët. 10, 392.—
In partic., to sharpen or quicken mentally, to incite, encourage, stimulate, inflame: velim cohortere et exacuas Cluatium,: aliquem (opp. deterrere),: aliquem irā,: se ad amorem immortalitatis,: animos in bella,: mentem varia ad conamina,.—Poet.: palatum (sapor),.

la:verb:exaudio.gloss: to hear, discern or perceive clearly
senses: to hear, discern or perceive clearly
to listen to, hearken, heed; obey; grant
la:verb:exaudio.html:
ex-audĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a.
To hear or perceive clearly (class.): Nec satis exaudiebam, nec sermonis fallebar tamen, Quae loquerentur,; cf. ; ; : cum aliquantulum progressus esset, subito exaudivit hinnitum,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 8, 33 et saep.: maxima voce, ut omnes exaudire possint, dico semperque dicam,; cf. ; ; ; ; .—With acc. and inf., .—
Less freq. in the signif. of audio.
To hear, perceive by hearing: quam multa, quae nos fugiunt in cantu, exaudiunt in eo genere exercitati,: exaudi, vultusque attolle jacentes,: tum denique saxa non exauditi rubuerunt sanguine vatis,: Haec vix proximis exaudientibus dixerat,: fingere cinctutis non exaudita Cethegis, .—Poet.: licet has exaudiat herbas (i. e. hos cantus),.—
To hearken, listen to; to regard, grant: tantum miserere precesque Supplicis exaudi,; so, preces,; : dirae exauditae ab omnibus diis,: vota precesque,; : vota populi,: quae optamus,.—Absol., ; ; ; et saep.—
To give heed to, to obey: ridebit monitor non exauditus,: exaudi,.—
To understand, comprehend = intellegere: nomina,; cf. verba,.
la:verb:exaudio.inflection: īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a.

senses: to rage, blaze forth, burst forth, flare up, become fired, inflamed, excited
la:verb:exardesco.html:
ex-ardesco, arsi, arsum, 3,
v. inch. n., qs. to blaze out, i. e. to kindle, take fire (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense and in Cic.; cf.: ardeo, ferveo, caleo, flagro, candeo, uro, etc., incendor, inflammor, etc.).
Lit.: nulla materies tam facilis ad exardescendum est, quae, etc.,: sulphur exardescens,.—
Transf., of the sun's heat: exarsit dies,.—And of a fiery color: fulgor carbunculi exardescens,.—
Trop., to be kindled, inflamed, to break out (in a good and bad sense).
Of personal subjects: exarsit iracundia ac stomacho,; cf. : (Induciomarus) multo gravius hoc dolore exarsit, * : infestius Papirium exarsurum,; cf. graviter,: haud secus exarsit quam Circo taurus aperto,: adeo exarserant animis,; so, animis,: libidinibus indomitis,: in omni genere amplificationis,: hodierno die ad spem libertatis exarsimus,: ad cupiditatem libertatis recuperandae,; : ad bellum,; : plebes ad id maxime indignatione exarsit,; cf.: ad quod exarsit adeo, ut, etc.,: milites in perniciosam seditionem exarsuri,; cf.: in iras,; : in proelium,.—Of the passion of love: in C. Silium ita exarserat (Messalina), .—
Of impersonal and abstract subjects: immane quantum animi exarsere, (p. 229 ed. Gerl.): ex quo exardescit sive amor, sive amicitia,; cf.: novum atque atrox proelium,: admirabilis quaedam benevolentiae magnitudo,: ira,; cf.: iracundia exercitus in eum,: ambitio,; : violentia Turni,: dolor Alcidae, et saep.: injuria,: bellum,; ; ; cf.: certamina inter patres plebemque,: seditio,: tanta ista importunitas inauditi sceleris,: fames auri, et saep.: tum propter multorum delicta etiam ad innocentium periculum tempus illud exarserat,: altercatio ex iracundia muliebri in contentionem animorum exarsit,; cf.: studia in proelium,: Corinthiorum vasorum pretia in immensum exarsisse,i. e. had risen,; cf.: quibus initiis in tantum admiratio haec exarserit, prooem. § 2: ira, (See also excandefacio and incendo.)!*? * Part. perf.: exarsus, a, um, burned up: res vestras incendio exarsas esse,.

la:verb:exardeo.html:
ex-ardĕo, ēre, 2, v. a. (eccl. Lat.).
Prop., to burn: ignis,; cf. ; .—
Trop., of the feelings, to be inflamed, blaze out: in brevi ira,: in desideriis suis,.

la:verb:exaresco.html:
ex-āresco, rŭi, 3,
v. inch. n., to dry up, become completely dry (rare, but class.).
Lit.: vestimenta uvida,: frumentum,: silva omnis radicitus,: amnes,; ; cf. fontes, * : lacus et stagna,: lacrimae,to dry up,.—
Trop.: neque dum exarui ex amoenis rebus et voluptariis,: sic omnis fetus repressus, exustusque flos siti veteris ubertatis exaruit,: cum vetustate exaruit opinio,dried up, extinguished,; cf.: vetus urbanitas,: facultas orationis,.

la:noun:exactio.html:
exactĭo, ōnis, f.
exigo
. *
A driving out, expelling: (regum), (perh. only on account of the preceding exactis regibus).—
A demanding, exacting, requisition.
In gen.: in exhibendis operariis,: quotidiana, operis,.—Hence, the supervision, conduct of a public work; cf. exactor, II. A.: operum publicorum,.—Far more freq.,
In partic., a calling in, collecting of debts, ; ; ; : vectigalium,, 28 et saep.—
Transf., a tax, tribute, impost: acerbissima capitum atque ostiorum,poll and hearth tax,: publicae, Asin. Pol. ap. ; cf. illicitae,; and: exactionum coactor (pater Horatii), Suet. Vita Hor.—
A finishing, completion, ; ; .

la:verb:exaestuo.gloss: to boil up, foam up, or ferment
senses: to boil up, foam up, or ferment
la:verb:exaestuo.html:
ex-aestŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
, to boil up, foam up, ferment (not freq. till after the Aug. period; in Cic. and Caes. not at all).
Neut.
Lit.
In gen.: exaestuat mare,; : fretum,: unda ima verticibus,: Aetna fundo imo,: bitumen e terra,: Nilus in fossas,.—
In partic., to effervesce, to glow with heat: Aegyptus torrenti calore solis exaestuat,.— Absol.: ut exaestuarat,had overheated himself,—
Trop.: mens exaestuat irā,; so, irā,; ; : dolor exaestuat intus,; cf. ignis (amoris),; poet.: vates magno igni,.—
Act., to boil up with, to give forth, exhale (very rarely): hos igitur tellus omnes exaestuat aestus,; so, aestus,.
la:verb:exaestuo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

senses: breathless, as if near death, resulting from fear or terror; fainting
la:adj:exanimis.html:
ex-ănĭmis, e, and ex-ănĭmus, a, um (cf. Wagner ad ; the latter form common in the plur., of which the former has only exanimes, nom. and acc.), adj.
anima
,
lifeless, dead (mostly postAug.; not in Cic. and Caes.; cf.: inanimis, exanimatus, mortuus).
Lit.
Form exanimis: (columba) Decidit exanimis,; cf. : ut exanimem labentem ex equo Scipionem vidit,: aliquamdiu jacuit, et saep.: corpus,; ; ; ; ; ; : caro,; ; cf. artus,.—Poet.: gelidae exanimesque favillae,i. e. dead, extinguished,: hiems,i. e. calm, without wind,.—
Form exanimus: pueri,: nos juvenem exanimum ... vano maesti comitamur honore,: pacem me exanimis et Martis sorte peremptis Oratis?: partim exanimos ante vallum aut in amnem Rhenum proiciunt,: corpus exanimum,; so, corpus (corpora),; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—As subst.: exănĭma, ōrum, n., lifeless things, ; .—
Transf., half dead with fear, terrified, dismayed (very rare; only in form exanimis): audiit exanimis,; cf. ; ; .

la:verb:exanimo.gloss: to deprive of air or wind; deflate; weaken, exhaust
senses: to deprive of air or wind; deflate; weaken, exhaust
to deprive of life, kill, wear out
to be out of breath, be weakened or be exhausted
to be deprived of life, be killed, or be dead
to deprive of spirit or life; to deprive of breath, to wind, make breathless or take one’s breath away; to alarm, stun, or terrify greatly; to agitate or trouble
la:verb:exanimo.html:
ex-ănĭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To deprive of air or wind.
Lit.: folles, i. e. to press together, so as to force out the air, Auct. Aetnae, 560.—
Transf. (in pass.), to be out of breath, weakened, exhausted: simul fore ut duplicato cursu Caesaris milites exanimarentur et lassitudine conficerentur,: milites cursu ac lassitudine exanimati,; ; ; ; .—
Of impers. or abstr. things, to be weakened: (vini faex) celerrime exanimatur loco non incluso condita,loses its strength,: nolo verba exiliter exanimata exire, with feeble breath, i. e. lifeless, tame, .—
To deprive of life, to kill (freq. and class.).
Lit.: telum saepe nocentes Praeterit exanimatque indignos,: aliquem,; ; ; ; cf.: se taxo,—
In pass., to be deprived of life, be killed, to die: (Epaminondas) cum gravi vulnere exanimari se videret,; cf. ; so ; ; al.; cf. in the part. perf.: exanimatus,killed, dead, (with exanimis); ; and 3; ; ; fin. al. —
Trop., to deprive of life or spirit, toalarm or terrify greatly, to put out of one's senses with fright, horror, etc.; to agitate, trouble: vorsor in amoris rota miser, Exanimor, feror, differor, distrahor, diripior,: oratio haec me miseram exanimavit metu,; cf.: te metus exanimant judiciorum atque legum,: Decius torpidos somno insuper pavore exanimat,: adolescentulus sic initio accusationis exanimatus sum, ut, etc.,: me exanimant et interimunt hae voces Milonis,: Tulliae meae morbus et imbecillitas corporis me exanimat,: cur me querelis exanimas (= conturbas, summo maerore afficis) tuis?; cf. ; et saep.—In the part. perf.: exanimata metu,; cf. ; ; : non me fefellit, sensi; eo exanimatus fui,; ; ; ; ;

la:noun:examen.html:
ex-āmen, ĭnis, n.
for ex-agmen, from ex and ago; cf. contamino and contagies, flamen and flagrare
.
A multitude issuing forth or flying out, a swarm. Primarily and class. of a swarm of bees: res rusticae laetae sunt tum pecudum pastu, apium examinibus, florum omnium varietate,; so, apium,; ; et saep.; cf. ; ; fin. et saep.; ; ; ; et saep.—
Transf., a multitude, crowd, shoal, swarm (freq. only after the Aug. per.): locustarum,: piscium,: pullorum (arboris),: juvenum,: infantium,; cf. : vernarum,; cf. servorum,: Graium vatum,: stuprorum (i. e. feminarum stupratarum), (3, 30, 41 M.) et saep.—In late Lat. even of abstract things: malorum,: maerorum, id. fin.: aetatum,: dilationum, et saep.—
A means of examining; hence, the tongue of a balance (very rare): examen est ligula vel lignum, quod mediam hastam ad pondera adaequanda tenet, Schol. ; cf. Paul. ex : Juppiter ipse duas aequato examine lances Sustinet, ; .—
Trop., a weighing, consideration, examination: examenve improbum in illa Castiges trutina,: legum,; cf. vitae,.

senses: to exalt, amplify, heighten, magnify, exaggerate
la:verb:exaggero.html:
ex-aggĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to raise a mound, dam, or dike; to heap up (class.; cf.: acervo, coacervo, cumulo, aggero).

Lit.: aggesta humo planitiem,: terram,: clivum super capita columnarum,: locum operibus,to surround with ramparts,: pluribus stramentis exaggerandum est aviarium,to be abundantly filled, supplied,.—

Transf., to enlarge, increase by heaping up: rem familiarem,; so, magnas opes,.—
Trop.: hic alteri alteris mortem morti exaggerabant, they mutually heaped up death upon death, Auct. B. Hisp. 5 fin.—Far more freq.,
Transf., to exalt, amplify, heighten, magnify, exaggerate: nihil est ad exaggerandam et amplificandam orationem accommodatius, quam, etc.,; cf.: oratio nimis alta et exaggerata (opp. humilis et abjecta),: quasi exaggerata altius oratio (with elatio et altitudo orationis),: artem oratione,; cf. beneficium verbis,: immanitatem parricidii vi orationis,: injuriam nostram,: animus excelsus et altus et virtutibus exaggeratus,: Xenocrates exaggerans tanto opere virtutem, extenuans cetera et abiciens,: auctae exaggerataeque fortunae,: juventam alicujus honoribus,. Hence, *
exaggĕranter, adv., with many words, .—
exaggĕrā-tus, a, um, P. a., cumulated, heightened, elevated (very seldom): exaggerata verborum volubilitate,.—Comp., ; cf. ib. § 9.

senses: to stir up, shake up, disturb
to attack (with criticism); criticise, censure, rail at, scold
la:verb:exagito.html:
ex-ăgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.,
to drive out of its position or place; to stir up, rouse up, disturb.
Lit. (very seldom): ut quicquid faecis subsederit exagitet, et in summum reducat,: vis (venti) exagitata foras erumpitur,. —Poet.: lustra ferarum Venatu,to disturb,: lepus hic aliis exagitandus erit,to rouse, start,; cf. .—
Trop., to rouse up (qs. like a wild beast), to disquiet, harass, persecute, disturb, torment.
In gen.: insectandis exagitandisque nummariis judicibus,; cf. : permulti sedes suas patrias, istius injuriis exagitati, reliquerant,: ab Suevis complures annos exagitati bello premebantur et agricultura prohibebantur,; cf. fin.: at omnes di exagitent me, si, etc.,; cf. : exagitari verberibus Furiarum,: quos flagitium, egestas, conscius animus exagitabat,: senatus vulgi rumoribus exagitatus,: rem publicam seditionibus,.—
In partic.
To scold, rail at, to attack violently, to censure, criticise, satirize, rally (cf.: objurgo, improbo, increpo, vitupero, calumnior, reprehendo; peto, incuso, etc.): hi omnes convicio L. Lentuli consulis correpti exagitabantur,: cum etiam Demosthenes exagitetur ut putidus,; cf. : inventi sunt, qui hanc dicendi exercitationem exagitarent atque contemnerent,: in rebus palam a consularibus exagitatis et in summam invidiam adductis,; cf. Cael. ap. : exagitabantur omnes ejus fraudes atque fallaciae,; cf. : quod apud Lucilium scite exagitat in Albucio Scaevola, quam lepide lexeis compostae, etc.,.—
To stir up, irritate, excite: coepere (tribuni) senatum criminando plebem exagitare,; cf. vulgum,.—In a good sense: hujus disputationibus et exagitatus maxime orator est et adjutus,incited, urged onwards,.—Of abstract objects: in tali tempore tanta vis hominis leniunda quam exagitanda videbatur,; .—
Transf., to stir up, excite the passions themselves: ne et meum maerorem exagitem et te in eundem luctum vocem, ; tristes curas,: furores immiti corde,.

la:verb:examino.html:
exāmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
[examen]. *
(acc. to examen, I.).— Neut., to form swarms, to swarm: examinant alvi,.—
(acc. to examen, II.).
Lit.
Act., to weigh (class.): (aër) tamquam paribus examinatus ponderibus,; cf.: ad certum pondus, * .—*
Neut.: alicui, to be in equilibrium with a thing, to counterbalance, counterpoise, .—
Trop., act., to weigh, ponder, consider, examine, try, test (class.): non aurificis statera, sed quadam populari trutina examinari,; cf.: omnia verborum momentis, non rerum ponderibus,; so, aliquid suis ponderibus,: diligenter verborum omnium pondera,; : emendate loquendi regulam,; juncturam syllabarum longarum et brevium aurium mensura,: (Parrhasius) examinasse subtilius lineas traditur (shortly after: circumscripsit omnia), Spald.: male verum examinat omnis Corruptus judex, * ; cf. of judicial examination,; ; . —Hence, exāmĭnātus, a, um, P. a., tried, i. e. careful, thoughtful (late Lat.): examinatissima diligentia,. —Adv.: exāmĭnātē, carefully, considerately: credere,.—Comp.: examinatius deliberare,.
la:verb:examino.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:noun:exactor.html:
exactor, ōris, m.
id.; cf. also exactio
. *
A driver-out, expeller: regum (Junii Valeriique),.—
A demander, exactor (cf.: redemptor, manceps, magister; also: publicanus, portitor).
In gen.: operis, i. e. an overseer, superintendent, enforcer of any kind of labor, ; cf. ; so, assiduus studiorum,; cf.: asper recte loquendi,: molestissimus sermonis Latini,: supplicii,an executioner,; cf. , and 3, 14 fin.; cf. .—
In partic., a collector of taxes, a tax gatherer, * ; ; Firm. 4, 3 al.; ; or of other debts due the state,. (Not in Cic.; but cf. exactio.)

la:verb:exalto.html:
ex-alto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
altus
(postAug.; mostly eccl. Lat.).
To raise, elevate, exalt: deus alia exaltat, alia submittit, prooem.: TERMINOS VETVSTATE COLLAPSOS,, no. 555: solium,.—
Trop.: exaltare, Deus,be praised,: vocem, et saep.—
To deepen: fodiunt (sulcos) et exaltant in tres pedes,: sulcum,: orbem ablaqueationis,.

la:noun:exauditio.html:
exaudītĭo, ōnis, f.
exaudio, II. B.
,
a hearkening to, granting: oratio exauditione dei dignior,; Chron. 33, 19.

la:noun:exaltatio.html:
exaltātĭo, ōnis, f.
exalto
.
Exaltation, elevation (eccl. Lat.): ab exaltatione tua dispersae sunt gentes,. —
Trop., pride, haughtiness: non congruit professoribus humilitatis,; cf. oculorum,: stultorum,.

la:noun:examinatio.html:
exāmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f.
examino
.
Lit., i. q. libratio, an equipoise, equilibrium, .—
Trop., a weighing, examination (post-class.), ; fin.

la:verb:exaperio.html:
ex-ăpĕrĭo, īre, v. a.,
to open wide, throw open (very rare): exapertae repente delubri fores, et audita major humana vox,: implicatissimam nodositatem,to undo, unloose,.

la:verb:exarmo.html:
ex-armo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to deprive of arms, to disarm (post-Aug.).
Lit.: cohortes,: dextras,: Medos,; ; cf. .—
Transf.
Navem, i. e. to unrig, dismantle, ; .—Absol., to lose the rigging of a ship: et si exarmavit, tamen reliquias navigii aptat ad cursum,; cf. .—
(Causa pro effectu.) To deprive of strength, to weaken: serpentem diro veneno,i. e. to render harmless,; so, taurum,: tigres,: aequor (terrae cingentes),: Romani exarmati,weakened, Ruhnk.—
Trop., to disarm: filium mater Veturia lacrimis suis exarmavit, Duker.; cf.: nautas mirabili forma,: accusationem,.

la:verb:exacerbo.html:
ex-ăcerbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (not anteAug.).
To exasperate, irritate, provoke, make angry; to grieve, afflict: ut recenti aliqua ira exacerbarentur animi,; ; ; 8, 33; ; ; ; —
In jurid. Lat., to aggravate, increase a punishment: supplicia,; cf.: crimen verbis impiis,; pass. impers.: crimine majestatis facto maxime exacerbatur in milites,.

la:verb:exaequo.html:
ex-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To make even or level with any thing.
Lit. (very rarely): inferior pars (ex transtillis) sub aqua exaequanda, etc.,: tumulos tumulis exaequabant, Auct. B. Hisp. 5 fin.—
Transf.: aurum auro expendetur, argentum argento exaequabitur,shall be balanced, compensated,.—Freq. and class.,
Trop., to place on a level, regard as equal, to equal: ii, qui sunt in amicitiae conjunctionisque necessitudine superiores, exaequare se cum inferioribus debent,; cf.: neminem secum dignitate, * ; ; cf.: vetus miles tironi liber voloni sese exaequari sineret,; so, aliquem alicui,; : nos caelo (victoria),: facta dictis,i. e. to relate the events with historic accuracy just as they occurred, Kritz.: uti militibus exaequatus cum imperatore labos volentibus esset,: ad hanc regulam omnem vitam tuam exaequa,conform,: qui omnia jura pretio exaequasset,; cf.: certamina belli ferro,: libertatem,: periculum,.—
To equal, be equal to any one; with acc. (cf. aequo): ut longitudo aut plenitudo harum (syllabarum) multitudinem alterius assequatur et exaequet,: tetricas Sabinas,.

la:verb:exaugeo.html:
ex-augĕo, ēre, v. a.,
to increase exceedingly (rare): amplius, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 270 ed. Vahlen): benefacta majorum tuorum exauge,; : opinionem,.

la:verb:exaedifico.html:
ex-aedĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To finish building, to build up, erect, construct (rare but class.).
Lit.: oppidum, * ; cf. : Capitolium (with efficere), : domos et villas,: templa deum,: hibernacula,; navem,: hunc mundum,—
Trop., to finish, complete: ne graveris exaedificare id opus, quod instituisti,; cf.: suam incohatam ignaviam,.—*
To turn out of doors: me ex his aedibus,.

senses: to endure to the end, exhaust
la:verb:exanclo.html:
ex-anclo (less accurately -antlo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (an archaic word; mostly ante-class.; cf. ),
to draw or bring out as a servant.
Lit.
In gen.: clavum, Pac. ap. .—
In partic., to draw out a liquid = exhaurio: vinum poculo pauxillulo saepe,.—Poet.: nisi patrem materno sanguine exanclando ulciscerer, i. e. spilling, shedding = effundendo, Enn. ap. (R), exanclare, effundere, Non. ib.—
Trop., to go through, suffer, endure something (esp. a misfortune, grievance): clades impatibiles, Att. ap. (R): aerumnas, labores,: quantis cum aerumnis illum exanclavi diem, Enn. ap. (Rib.

Trag. Fragm. p. 26); cf.: tot belli annos, Cic. poet. Div. 2, 30, 64 (as a translation of Hom. Il. 2, 328): o multa dictu gravia, perpessu aspera, quae corpore exanclata atque animo pertuli! id. poët. Tusc. 2, 8, 20 (translation of Soph. Trach. 1048).—In prose in Cicero (perh. only as a poet. reminiscence): Herculi quendam laborem exanclatum a Carneade, etc.,.—Hence,

To endure to the end, exhaust: cum exanclavisset omnes labores, tum, etc.,: fere exanclavimus Tyranni saevom ingenium, Att. ap. (R).

la:noun:exanimatio.html:
exănĭmātĭo, ōnis, f.
exanimo
.
